analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act, restoring pre-2010 insurance rules, with no replacement attached.
analysis.headline: The House passed a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act 239–186 on a nearly party-line vote, but the Senate never took it up and the bill died there.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and its companion law in full, effective 180 days after enactment, and restore the insurance rules that existed before 2010. That would end the coverage expansions (Medicaid expansion, premium tax credits), the protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and the taxes that finance the law, including surtaxes on high-income households. It directs House committees to draft replacement bills at some later date, but attaches no replacement to the repeal itself. The House passed it on February 3, 2015; the Senate read it twice and placed it on its calendar, where it sat without a vote until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most directly, since repeal erases the Affordable Care Act's 3.8% investment-income surtax and 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax on top earners. Medical device makers, tanning businesses, and brand-name drug makers gain from the repeal of the health-industry fees and taxes that helped fund the law. Health insurers gain freedom from the law's rules on pricing, minimum medical-loss ratios, and guaranteed coverage of sick people, letting them return to denying or surcharging coverage based on health status and gender.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, and medical-device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA and the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act 180 days after enactment, and restores the provisions of law the two statutes amended or repealed.
Repeal ends the ACA's taxes and fees, including the surtaxes on high-income households that helped pay for coverage expansions and industry fees on medical devices and brand-name drugs.
It exempts the bill's budgetary effects from the statutory pay-as-you-go scorecards, so the deficit cost of repeal is not counted against pay-as-you-go enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: The people who gained coverage and protections under the ACA bear the cost: people who bought subsidized marketplace plans, adults added to Medicaid in expansion states, people with pre-existing conditions who would again face denial or unaffordable premiums, young adults who could stay on a parent's plan until 26, Medicare beneficiaries who had lower drug costs, and patients using free preventive services. The roughly $1 trillion-plus of revenue repealed also had to be replaced or the deficit grows; the bill instead exempts its cost from pay-as-you-go rules. Repeal would take effect 180 days after enactment with no replacement enacted, leaving a gap.

drawbacks.text: The repeal would take effect 180 days after enactment while any replacement is only a promise that House committees 'shall report' legislation later; nothing in the bill guarantees a replacement passes or that coverage does not lapse in the meantime.

Restoring pre-2010 law would again allow insurers to deny coverage or set premiums based on pre-existing conditions and gender, undoing guaranteed-issue and community-rating protections for sick and older patients.

Repealing the law's dedicated revenues while keeping Medicare spending growth would widen deficits; the bill sidesteps statutory pay-as-you-go enforcement by ordering that its budgetary effects not be entered on the PAYGO scorecards.

House Democrats' motion to recommit — which would have blocked repeal if insurers could again discriminate on pre-existing conditions or gender, if Medicare Part D costs rose, or if middle-class families lost premium tax credits — was rejected 179–241.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The concentrated gains are real but narrow: tax relief for the top few percent of earners and fee relief for a few health industries. The losses are broad: repeal strips coverage and price protections from millions of marketplace buyers, Medicaid expansion enrollees, and people with pre-existing conditions, and it does so on a fixed 180-day clock with no replacement attached, only an instruction to committees to draft one later. The bill's design — full repeal first, replacement promised, cost exempted from pay-as-you-go enforcement — would have shifted risk to patients while locking in the tax cuts.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 239–186 in February 2015, but the Senate only read it twice and placed it on its calendar; no vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on February 3, 2015 by a recorded vote of 239–186, with 239 of 245 Republicans voting yes and no Democrat voting yes (3 Republicans voted no).
House Democrats' motion to recommit with instructions to protect pre-existing-condition coverage, Medicare Part D costs, and premium tax credits failed 179–241, with 240 of 245 Republicans voting no.

The Senate received the bill on February 4, 2015, read it a first and second time, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 14); the record shows no further Senate action.
The bill's Senate calendar placement carried through the rest of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017, without a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The ACA's beneficiaries kept their coverage and protections, and the industries and high earners who would have gained from repeal did not. Senate leaders also avoided a recorded vote on a full repeal that polls at the time showed to be unpopular.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA beneficiaries; senators avoided a vote

for.name: Rep. Bradley Byrne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on January 28, 2015.

for.name: House Rules Committee and Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Reported a closed rule (H. Res. 70) that barred amendments and brought the bill to the floor for a vote six days after introduction.

against.name: 183 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage and backed a motion to recommit that would have conditioned repeal on keeping pre-existing-condition protections and premium tax credits.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote after it was placed on the calendar.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed repeal of his signature health law; a veto was assured had the bill reached his desk.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: Republicans voted 239–3 for passage and Democrats voted 0–183 against; the motion to recommit was 179–241, with 179 of 188 Democrats voting yes and no Republicans.

industries.note: Repeal frees insurers from guaranteed issue, community rating, minimum medical-loss ratios, and marketplace rules — restoring the ability to charge sick people more or deny them coverage — while also ending the individual mandate and subsidies that brought insurers millions of subsidized customers. Historically, the pricing freedom gained by repeal comes at the direct expense of people in poor health.

Repeal erases the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax on high earners, which were the law's main financing for coverage expansions. The benefit flows to the top few percent of earners; the cost is borne by the people who lose coverage.

Repeal lifts the ACA's excise tax on medical devices, a direct windfall to the industry that partially financed the law. Device prices would be unchanged for consumers; only the industry's tax bill drops.

Repeal lifts the ACA's fee on brand-name prescription drugs, but also ends the required discounts for seniors who hit the Medicare coverage gap, so seniors would pay more for drugs while the industry pays less in fees.

Repeal ends the ACA's cuts to Medicare uncompensated-care payments but also removes the coverage expansions that sharply reduced hospitals' uninsured caseloads, leaving hospitals facing more unpaid care again.
